*Chunk 1*: Loading the required packages, including the tidyverse for data manipulation. Although I loaded terra and sf, I only used sf once to load in Australia's borders, and I did not use terra. I originally intended to do a more spatially-focused analysis for this data sprint; however, I was limited by data availability and my own ability. I will certainly work to improve in the spatial analysis area.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(terra)
library(sf)
```

*Chunk 2*: In this chunk, I utilized Dr. Shannon's script to read in the numbats data and weather data (using the weatherOz package). It appears that this chunk works to first manipulate the numbats data -- including via the addition of a 0 to the month data to put it in a format consistent with the weather data. From there, weather data is extracted using the SILO API to get a more complete record of weather data -- given that the weather data provided in the numbat sightings is very incomplete. After that, an attempt was made to join the weather and numbat datasets; however, the lack of an exact-matching field with which the join could be peformed made this task difficult (and thus it was not completed).  

```{r}
#Using Dr. Shannon's script to get wx data in:

install.packages("weatherOz")
library(weatherOz)

numbat_data<-read_csv("data/numbats.csv") %>%
  filter(!is.na(eventDate)) %>%
  mutate(event_oz=paste0(year(eventDate),
                         str_pad(month(eventDate),2,pad="0"),
                         str_pad(day(eventDate),2,pad="0")))
summary(numbat_data)

x <- get_data_drill(
  longitude  = 153.0,
  latitude   = -27.5,
  start_date = "20240101",
  end_date   = "20241231",
  values     = c("max_temp", "min_temp", "rain"),
  api_key    = "jshannon@uga.edu"
)

numbat_wx<-function(row_sel){
  numbat_sel<-numbat_data[row_sel,]
  
  get_data_drill(
    longitude=numbat_sel$decimalLongitude,
    latitude=numbat_sel$decimalLatitude,
    start_date=numbat_sel$event_oz,
    end_date=numbat_sel$event_oz,
    values     = c("max_temp", "min_temp", "rain"),
    api_key    = "jshannon@uga.edu"
  ) %>%
    rename(decimalLatitude=latitude,
           decimalLongitude=longitude,)
}

#nrow_plus1 <- nrow(numbat_data) + 1 #Did not work, was trying to experiment with the dates

weather_data<-map_df(1:nrow(numbat_data),possibly(numbat_wx))
#numbat_wx<-numbat_data %>%
  #rename(date=day) %>%
  #left_join(weather_data)

```

*Chunk 3*: In this chunk, I aimed to plot the max temp and precip observations for each numbat sighting that recorded weather data. The goal of this, albeit very simple, exercise, was to determine if there was any meaningful pattern in either the temp or precip recorded on the days that numbats were spotted. 

To accomplish this, I first cleaned the numbats data (using the variable `numbats_cleaned`) to remove all observations that were missing data for precip or max temp. I then mutated the max temp readings (by dividing each value by 10) to get a decimal point into the reported values (as they previously lacked one, and were thus reporting temp values in the hundreds of degrees Celsius [i.e., the raw data listed the temp as 300°C, where the actual reading should be 30.0°C]). 

From there, I created a very simple visual (as given below the code chunk) that depicted the precip value (on the x-axis) and the max temp value (on the y-axis) for each numbat sighting. An analysis of that visualization is left for the discussion section. 

```{R}
#Trying to plot the data for numbat sightings vs. precip (in some way)

#Without the weather_data, just the wx data in numbat_data

numbats_cleaned <- numbat_data %>%
  filter(prcp != "NA") %>%
  filter(tmax != "NA") %>%
  mutate(tmax_corr = tmax/10)

ggplot(numbats_cleaned,
       aes(x=prcp, 
           y=tmax_corr)) +
  geom_point() +
  ggtitle("Precip and Max Temp Obs for Numbat Sightings") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 11)) +
  xlab("Mean Precip (mm)") +
  ylab("Mean Maximum Temp (°C)") #Had to do this to capitilize "region" in the legend. 

```

*Chunk 4*: In this chunk, I create a very similar (and again, very simple) graphic to show the max temp and precip data for all the weather data gathered in Chunk 2. An explanation of this graphic is provided in the discussion. 

```{R}
#Plotting the wx_data

ggplot(weather_data,
       aes(x=rainfall, 
           y=air_tmax)) +
  geom_point() +
  ggtitle("Precip and Max Temp Obs (Overall Weather Dataset)") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 11)) +
  xlab("Mean Precip (mm)") +
  ylab("Mean Maximum Temp (°C)") 
```

*Chunk 5*: Here, I begin by loading in a simple shapefile of Australia's borders (using the original `australia_borders` variable) using st_read. However, Will (2) showed me an even more intuitive way of getting that geographic information (apparently also including a shaded area for the country, using the map_data function), so I ended up using data from that source. I only maintained the previous version of data retreival for reference purposes. 

After that, I created another plot that leverages the above-mentioned Australia geographic information to plot numbat observations across the country. The numbat sightings are given by the black dots. 

It should also be noted that I attempted to find a raster of Australia precip data to overlay onto this map -- just to demonstrate that numbats tend to live in areas devoid of precip (which also makes sense on an intuitive sense) -- however, I ran into data availability and time constraints. Nevertheless, I did attach an image to my repo that contains that precip data (just for reference). That file is titled "Australia precip data_Australia BOM" and is sourced from the Australia Bureau of Meteorology.

Further, it should be noted that all the numbat observations that had meteorological data occurred in the extreme SW part of Australia. I included rthe remainder of the observations for reference. 

```{R}
#Trying to plot the numbat obs on a map of Australia to prove the obvious -- numbats are found in desert areas that, unsurprisingly, do not get much rain. 

#australia_borders <- st_read("data/AUSTRALIA SHAPEFILE/AUSTRALIA_Shapefiles/Australia_adm/Australia_adm01.shp") %>%
  #st_transform(4326)

australia_borders <- map_data("world",region = "Australia")

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data=australia_borders,
               aes(x=long,
                   y=lat,
                   group=group,
                   alpha=0.5)) +
  geom_point(data=numbat_data,
             aes(x=decimalLongitude,
                 y=decimalLatitude)) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(title = "Numbat Sightings in Australia")

```

**Discusssion**

*Introduction*
A brief description of the dataset and its main variables.
The research question you are trying to answer related to this dataset. 

Response: For this activity, I utilized the numbats dataset we chose in class. This dataset includes data on numbat sightings across Australia, including their location, scientific name, date, and a limited amount of weather data (like temp and precip). 

The research question I was attempting to answer was examining the relationship between numbat sightings and weather conditions. My original question was trying to just evaluate the relationship between numbats and precip amounts; however, I pivoted to the above mentioned question (looking at the broader relationship between numbat sightings and weather observations). Specifically, I eventually attempted to answer whether there is any difference in temp and precip distribution for numbat sightings compared to the overall temp and precip distribution. 

*Analysis*
A section in which you answer that question using R coding skills you've learned. This will include code chunks as well as brief description of what each of those code chunks is doing.
This section should include at least two visualizations (graphs/maps) relevant to your research question.

Response: The analysis of my code chunks -- and my visualizations -- is provided above. 

*Discussion*
Explains how you would answer your research question based on your analysis. Make specific reference to the results in your analysis section that support this answer.

Response: Based on my analysis section, I found that the max temp and precip distributions for numbat sightings does not vary meaningfully from the overall distribution of those variables. This is demonstrated by the fact that there is a very similar distribution of both variables between my first and second visualization (using the numbat weather data and overall weather data, respectively). I should note that I have very low confidence in the values reported -- especialy for precip -- in the numbats dataset, given that this data appears to report rainfall that is far higher than given in the overall weather data from SILO (including one observation well over 90 mm, when the overall weather data has no observations anywhere close to that value). In any case, the general distribution appears to be the same, suggesting that there is no meaningful difference between the weather numbats prefer and the overall spread of weather in those areas that numbats are sighted. 

In the end, this finding is not particularly interesting or surprising -- and certainly indicates to me that I should've chosen better methods and/or a better question.
